questions.html: Explain the context of: Remember Caesar.
questions.answer: The note is found in Weston’s pocket. He misreads it as a threat, though it is only a reminder about a visitor.

questions.html: Explain the context of: They don't assassinate nobodies.
questions.answer: Lady Weston says this to tease her husband when he panics about being targeted by assassins.

questions.html: Explain the context of: The last time it was in danger you had been eating game pie.
questions.answer: Lady Weston says this when Weston tells her his life is in danger, showing her witty disbelief.

questions.html: Explain the context of: The last time it was in danger you had been eating game pie.
questions.answer: Lady Weston says this when Weston announces that his life is in grave danger. Her remark shows her wit and disbelief.

questions.html: Explain the context of: What was in the parcel, do you think?
questions.answer: Weston asks this at the end after learning that the package was not a bomb. It is the final comic reversal.

questions.html: What does Ides of March refer to in the play?
questions.answer: It refers to 15 March, the day Julius Caesar was assassinated.

questions.html: What does flippancy suggest in Lady Weston’s speech?
questions.answer: It suggests a light, humorous attitude that dismisses Weston’s panic.

questions.html: What does infernal machine mean in Weston’s imagination?
questions.answer: He thinks it is a bomb or disguised explosive device.

questions.html: What does irrelevant and inconsiderable minutiae reveal about Weston?
questions.answer: It shows that he is irritated by Lady Weston’s attention to small practical details even while he himself is panicking.

questions.html: What does the ending reveal about Weston’s mistake?
questions.answer: It reveals that the whole crisis was caused by Weston’s absent-mindedness and imagination.

questions.html: How is Lord Weston introduced in the play?
questions.answer: He is introduced as pompous, proud and full of his own importance, but also as an absent-minded man who misreads ordinary events.

questions.html: Why is Roger’s character comic?
questions.answer: Roger is conscientious but absent-minded. He listens, works and obeys, yet he often misses the obvious, which adds to the humour.

questions.html: What role does Lady Weston play in the comedy?
questions.answer: She acts as Weston’s witty opposite. Her calm teasing exposes his panic and keeps the scene light.

questions.html: Why does Weston think he is in danger?
questions.answer: He finds a note saying Remember Caesar and connects it with Caesar’s murder on the Ides of March. That makes him imagine an assassination plot.

questions.html: What happens to the parcel and why is it funny?
questions.answer: Weston and Roger treat it as a bomb, but it is only Weston’s new cloak. The mismatch between panic and reality makes it comic.

questions.html: How does the play create suspense?
questions.answer: The play uses Weston’s fear, the sealed doors, the package, the pistol and the knock at the door to build suspense before revealing the harmless truth.

questions.html: What is the significance of Mr Caesar’s visit?
questions.answer: His visit exposes Weston’s mistake completely. The supposed assassin is merely a gardener with an appointment.

questions.html: What does the title contribute to the play?
questions.answer: The title sounds serious, but in the play it becomes comic because Caesar is only the name of the gardener Weston was expecting.

questions.html: How does the play treat the idea of reputation?
questions.answer: Weston imagines that his reputation makes him a target. The play gently mocks his vanity by showing how small the real situation is.

questions.html: Why is the ending humorous?
questions.answer: The ending is humorous because Weston’s whole alarm turns out to be pointless. The parcel is a cloak and the visitor is the gardener.

questions.html: Remember Caesar is a light-hearted comedy. Discuss.
questions.answer: The play is comic because it is driven by Weston’s false alarm. A harmless reminder turns into a fear of assassination, then into panic about a bomb, and finally into embarrassment when the visitor and the parcel are explained. The title, the dialogue and the repeated misunderstandings all support the humour.

questions.html: Compare the character traits of Lord Weston and his wife.
questions.answer: Weston is pompous, vain, anxious and self-important. Lady Weston is calm, witty, practical and amused by his excesses. Their contrast creates much of the play’s humour.

questions.html: How does the play depend on mistaken identity and irony?
questions.answer: Weston mistakes a reminder for a warning, a parcel for a bomb and the gardener’s name for an assassin’s message. The audience sees the harmless truth long before Weston does, which creates dramatic irony and comedy.

questions.html: What is the role of Roger in the play’s humour?
questions.answer: Roger is dutiful but slow to grasp the situation. His literal obedience makes Weston’s panic look even more absurd, and his careful seriousness contrasts with the ridiculousness of the crisis.

questions.html: Discuss the importance of the title Remember Caesar.
questions.answer: The title sounds threatening because it evokes Julius Caesar’s assassination. But in the play it refers to a simple reminder for a gardener named Caesar. The gap between the title’s gravity and the actual meaning is a major source of irony.

questions.html: Why is Lady Weston important to the structure of the play?
questions.answer: She prevents the play from becoming heavy or fearful. Her quick responses, practical comments and teasing tone keep the comedy moving and help expose Weston’s exaggerated imagination.

questions.html: How does the play show that fear can create its own problems?
questions.answer: Weston’s imagination makes him treat the note, the package and the knock at the door as threats. Because of his fear, he turns ordinary household events into a comic emergency.
